beats.text: Here is one AI model. It catches ninety percent of sick patients, and correctly clears ninety percent of healthy ones. Let's use it on three different populations.
First, a population where half the people have the disease. Five hundred out of a thousand.
The model raises four hundred and fifty true alarms, and fifty false ones. So when it says alarm, it is right ninety percent of the time. That is the P P V.
Now a population where only ten percent are sick. One hundred people.
It catches ninety of them. But nine hundred healthy people means ninety false alarms. P P V drops to fifty percent. A coin flip.
And now a rare condition. Just one percent. Ten people.
It catches nine. But it also raises ninety-nine false alarms. Only about eight percent of its alarms are real.
Same model. Same sensitivity, same specificity. But the rarer the condition, the lower the P P V. That is prevalence at work.
Now, one more trap. Take that rare condition again: ten sick people in a thousand.
Imagine a lazy model that simply says: nobody is sick.
It is right nine hundred and ninety times out of a thousand. Ninety-nine percent accurate!
And it found nobody. Sensitivity: zero.
So on imbalanced data, accuracy can fool you. Always ask what happens to the patients the model gets wrong.
